title: The Army Secretary Resigns: The People Who Know How to Fight Get Cleared Out First
dek: Twenty-five years after 9/11, the U.S. military has been on a treadmill: budgets eaten by war, transformation forced through on cheap technology, and the officers who actually understand tech and are willing to take risks are being cleared out batch by batch.
why: The first half — the 9/11 reckoning and Army personnel insider detail — is dense with information; the second half, on AI battlefields and model distillation, is more casual chat, so you can listen to just the first half.
who: Practitioners tracking U.S. defense budgets, service personnel and procurement, and defense-tech investors who need to judge the window for U.S. military transformation.
skip: The farewell song after 01:03:40 can be skipped; the AI battlefield section before it is also low on information density.

points.h: The war on terror ate the money for military transformation
points.body: Before 9/11 the U.S. military was transforming as Rumsfeld demanded, under the expectation of a relatively comfortable budget environment in which new technology could be slowly inserted into the force. Then GWAT arrived, all available resources were sucked into the war, and the transformation directive remained while the money was gone. The result was a run of procurement disasters: the Army's Future Combat Systems, the Navy's Ford-class carrier, the Littoral Combat Ship, DDG-1000 Zumwalt, and the CGX that was simply never built. Brian's judgment is that the technology jumped too far, the investment was far too little, and everyone was distracted supporting a war that had just started, so these programs were doomed to fail. The troubles with today's B-21 and F-35 trace back to this period too.

points.h: Twenty-five years on a treadmill, never actually stopping
points.body: Tony points out that op-tempo never stopped after it started in 2001: 12-month, 15-month deployment rotations, and the National Guard is still deploying both domestically and overseas today. Killing Bin Laden in 2011 could have been a high point, but nothing changed afterward — deployments continued, and through the fall of Kabul, they were still deploying. No one has fully calculated what 25 straight years in that state costs an army. Brian adds a mechanism: in the past, conventional forces trained at home, reset, and went through a training progression, and that rhythm disappeared, replaced by "preparing for the next deployment," so there is no time to test new technology or study new ways of fighting.

points.h: MRAP thinking: use a bigger truck to stop anti-tank missiles
points.body: Brian gives an example absurd in its specificity. In Syria, the threat was not IEDs but ATGMs (anti-tank guided weapons, similar to Russian TOW variants). The commander's reflex, however, was to stuff everyone into MRAPs — making the vehicles bigger only made it easier for ATGMs to find targets, and MRAP armor cannot stop munitions designed to penetrate tanks. His conclusion: risk calculation in the war-on-terror era has gone so deep that commanders cannot reconceptualize even a small tactical adjustment. This is also the direct consequence of why many commanders today struggle to adapt to Ukraine and the Lisko battlefield and find it hard to imagine how tactics will change.

points.h: Get used to zero casualties and you can't accept that people will die
points.body: Brian says that after 9/11 the U.S. military became increasingly risk- and casualty-averse. The Littoral Combat Ship debate is the specimen: opponents said the ship couldn't take a hit and would be sunk the moment war started; the original proposers answered that it was never going to be sent into a major war, and if it were ambushed and sunk, that was the risk you take as a soldier. That logic was completely unacceptable on Capitol Hill — Iraq and Afghanistan pushed casualties far below the levels of past wars, everyone got used to it, and so they cannot accept that facing a peer opponent will in all likelihood mean a lot of dead. The result is continued construction of "Death Star"-style large ships and large platforms, hoping they can protect themselves, rather than going with smaller, more distributed routes that accept a different risk structure.

points.h: Twenty-five years surrounding Iran, but no network built
points.body: Brian says this is the most important lesson he learned from 9/11, from a friend's reminder: for 25 years the U.S. basically surrounded Iran, and the CIA and parts of special operations had the job of developing networks and identifying people who could oppose an oppressive regime, in case a moment of change came. But when the shooting war with Iran started six months ago, it looked like very little network and capability building had been done in those 25 years. The reason is a mental shift: GWAT focused on counterinsurgency and catching bad guys, not the long-term unconventional warfare of pre-positioning for future conflict — how to support an insurgency inside a regime you might one day want to overthrow. In his words, everyone was too busy stabilizing the situation rather than destabilizing.

points.h: Driscoll resigns, and from here on it's all acting officials
points.body: Tony recaps: George was fired, Driscoll went to the White House, said "everything is terrible," and resigned that same week. The background is the Army being meddled with back and forth by OSD and the Secretary of the Army's office, plus personality clashes. What he hears is that Congress will not confirm anyone else Pete nominates, so either they bring in someone both the White House and Congress can accept but Pete doesn't like, or they just keep using acting officials. He judges this is the start of the rest of this administration being "stuck with acting officials": after the midterms the House will flip at least, the Senate will either flip or be 50:50, no one will have the energy to push this kind of person through, and so acting officials, continued OSD meddling, and low morale will persist.

points.h: The drone battalion is disbanded, and experimental capacity goes with it
points.body: The Army at the same time decided to disband the newly created drone battalion — a battalion that was supposed to directly absorb Ukraine's experience and then study how to embed it into infantry battalions. Tony acknowledges there is a good argument that "it shouldn't exist in just one battalion": concentrating lessons in a central repository deprives every commander of the responsibility to think about organization themselves. But his worry is that the Army still needs a unit that can run experiments, run tests, and allow failure; cutting it in the name of "uniformity" loses the ability to experiment, and the force will stand still. He also names Chris Donahue as sacrificed: a commander widely recognized as understanding technology, the effects of technology, and how to run international partnerships, done in because of the Abbey Gate bombing (not his fault) and a photo taken by a reporter.

points.h: Officers lose confidence in layers by rank
points.body: Tony breaks down morale by rank: junior officers are still early but already thinking "garrison isn't what I signed up for," and that not being in garrison means going out to take missiles; field-grade officers are starting to agonize over whether they have to make political decisions to stay; senior field-grade officers and junior generals are basically "either go all in or become completely disillusioned." He says the whole force is tired, and this doesn't look like the Army they joined. And in interviewees' words the Iran war is more of a tipping point than Donahue's departure — many O4 and O5 officers he knows originally supported this administration and were furious after the Donahue affair. Brian adds: people like Donahue are the true product of elite selection, and cutting them makes people doubt the claim of "promotion by ability alone."

points.h: A general's core function is to own risk for those below
points.body: Brian offers a mechanism: one of a general's most important roles is to own risk — to take on risk, thereby allowing experimentation and allowing subordinate units to try new things. Once a firing looks political, that channel is cut: which line do I cross to get fired or lose my command? So everything anyone wants to do stops. He also points to another pressure: the Army budget is being cut or flattened, with money going to new technology, other services, and the current Iran war. And people are the most expensive thing, so the most likely approach is to keep end strength unchanged and cut the money that supports people — fewer new weapons, worse readiness and training, less housing support, but flashy equipment still gets bought.

points.h: Fighting Iran uses the expensive munitions reserved for China
points.body: Brian lays out the chain of responsibility for the munitions shortage clearly: to avoid casualty risk, to stay low-profile, to avoid losses, the U.S. military struck Iran with the longest-range, most stealthy, expensive munitions — the ones that were reserved for China, now burned through. At the same time, to preserve follow-on strike options, airborne forces stayed there, and protecting them requires air-defense interceptors that were already scarce. So the munitions predicament was caused by operational decisions, and those decisions came from the secretary and the White House; Steve Feinberg just took the fall for the boss. Tony adds: acting officials who have not been confirmed by the Senate are limited in budget and authority, and if acting officials are everywhere, they can't even move money for this war.

points.h: Russian troops are using AI to fool Putin's own people
points.body: Tony cites a report from the Institute for the Study of War: Russian battalion and brigade levels are using AI to generate false information about the war, aimed at their own side, specifically at Putin. For months or even years before, the practice was to send two men with a Russian flag 15 kilometers past the front line, take a photo, and then either get killed or run back, to prove to Putin that they were advancing. The report says these commanders are now being punished for it, but that this happens very frequently. Tony's question is: are they punished because they got caught, or because they lied to Putin? He also worries this will in turn affect how people on this side of the ocean judge the state of the war and which sources they listen to. Justin adds that generative AI will become a routine layer of deception operations and strategic communications, and may even produce a "dead internet"-style total distrust.

points.h: The Houthis used Claude to write vehicle control software
points.body: Anthropic released a report listing how suspicious actors worldwide use Claude. One example: a Yemeni party used Claude Code to develop guidance, navigation and control software to maneuver and stabilize a vehicle; an outdoor test failed, and within hours these people were back asking Claude why it failed. Brian's comment: if you're going to do cyber warfare, why not just enter the opponent's OODA loop and use American software you can control in real time to influence the answers it gives. He also mentions that the prompt Chinese companies use to distill models is as simple as one line — "I am not for distillation" — and then the model complies; and that DeepSeek domestically routes queries to a relay station, hands them to Claude to answer, and returns them to the user, which is a double violation of China's own data compliance rules.
